       1             SENATOR SAVINO:  Good morning, everyone.

       2             I'm Senator Diane Savino.  For those of you

       3      who don't know me, I am the Chair of the

       4      Senate Committee on Children and Families.

       5             At some point today, I'm assuming we will be

       6      joined by some of the other members of the

       7      Senate Committee on Children and Families.

       8      Senator Duane, perhaps; Senator Montgomery.  We may

       9      even have a visit from Senator Squadron, who's

      10      upstairs on the 20th floor.

      11             But, for now, since we're here, this hearing

      12      is scheduled to start at 10 a.m.  I believe that we

      13      should proceed.

      14             The subject of the hearing today is

      15      child care; child care in New York City.  And it

      16      will take into consideration some concerns that

      17      have come out of the child care and community, and

      18      the day-care community, with respect to Early Learn.

      19             Our first testimony will be presented by

      20      Sara Vechiotti --

      21             SARA VECHIOTTI:  Perfect.

      22             SENATOR SAVINO:  Perfect.

      23             -- who is the acting deputy commissioner for

      24      child care and Head Start for New York City ACS.

      25             Following Sara will be, Raglan George, for





 

                                                                   6
       1      District Council 1707;

       2             And, behind them will be, Linda Manley, from

       3      the Lawyers Alliance for New York.

       4             Welcome, Sara; and you can proceed with your

       5      testimony.

       6             You don't have to read the whole testimony.

       7      If you want to summarize it, that's fine.  And, we

       8      have a list of questions that we're prepared to

       9      present to you, and I think you will be able to

      10      answer many of the questions that we're going to be

      11      presenting today.

      12             So, go ahead, Ms. Vechiotti.

      13             SARA VECHIOTTI:  Thank you.

      14             Good morning, Chair Savino, and members of

      15      the Committee on Children and Families.

      16             I am Sara Vechiotti, acting deputy

      17      commissioner of child care and Head Start at the

      18      Administration for Children Services.

      19             On behalf of Children Services,

      20      Commissioner Ronald E. Richter, I would like to

      21      thank you for the opportunity to be here today to

      22      speak with you about the issues involving

      23      child care in New York City.

      24             It is vitally important that the Committee on

      25      Children and Families is holding this hearing to





 

                                                                   7
       1      focus on challenges facing child care in

       2      New York State.

       3             Child care and early education are important

       4      supports for working families, and employment, in

       5      New York.  With those supports, many New Yorkers

       6      could not be part of the workforce.

       7             At the same time, child care and early

       8      education provide children with a solid foundation

       9      for appropriate development and education.  The

      10      lessons and skills learned by the children

      11      prepare them for school, and generate benefits far

      12      into their lives.

      13             The State of New York needs to fully support

      14      child care, to foster education and success of our

      15      youngest citizens, and to enable parents to

      16      continue to work, and, to reenter the job market.

      17             Children Services administers one of the

      18      largest publicly funded early care and education

      19      systems in the country, serving approximately

      20      120,000 children a year, which includes

      21      child care, Head Start, and universal

      22      pre-kindergarten.

      23             Subsidized child care administered by

      24      Children Services promotes family well-being, by

      25      allowing parents to pursue and maintain





 

                                                                   8
       1      employment, and by promoting child development.

       2             Currently, approximately 94,000 children are

       3      enrolled in the City's subsidized child-care system.

       4      The remaining children are served through the

       5      Head Start system.

       6             Of the families served in child care,

       7      approximately 65 percent are working families, and

       8      another 26 percent are families in education or

       9      training programs.

      10             Families are eligible for subsidized

      11      child care if they're receiving cash assistance, are

      12      served by the child-welfare system, are low-income

      13      employed, and meet certain other criteria.

      14             Child care is provided in a variety of

      15      settings.

      16             The largest percentage of children in

      17      child care are being served in center-based

      18      settings; followed by, informal family, friend,

      19      and neighbor care; and then, finally, followed by

      20      family child-care settings.

      21             As you know, in the last several years,

      22      Children Services has faced significant fiscal

      23      challenges in our efforts to maintain high-quality

      24      child care for families.

      25             For the City fiscal-year 2012, ACS faced a





 

                                                                   9
       1      sizable deficit of $95 million due to dramatic

       2      increases in the cost of providing child care and

       3      the loss of federal stimulus dollars.

       4             For example:  Costs in the voucher system are

       5      escalating, as families are increasingly using

       6      regulated child care and more younger children, aged

       7      infant to preschool, are being served.

       8             While these are both positive trends that we

       9      support, they are more costly.

      10             Other challenges for the system include,

      11      the new 2011 State child-care market rates, and

      12      rising insurance costs for the contracted system.

      13             At the same time, federal funding has not

      14      kept pace with the rising costs.

      15             As a consequence, Children Services faced a

      16      critical situation, where we had no choice but to

      17      reduce the number of child-care subsidies we can

      18      fund by approximately 16,500 children.

      19             In addition, Children Services, like other

      20      City agencies, needed to fulfill its responsibility

      21      to reduce spending to address the City's deficit;

      22      and one of the solutions increased parent fees for

      23      child care.

      24             Due to the efforts and support of Mayor and

      25      City Council, 82 million in one-time funding was





 

                                                                   10
       1      made available to the child-care budget.

       2             These one-time City-only funds were made

       3      available to avoid reductions which had been

       4      necessary, as the stimulus funds ended, insurance

       5      costs and market rates continued to rise, without

       6      corresponding increases in federal funds.

       7             The restoration meant that all children who

       8      benefited from child-care services, and were to be

       9      affected by the service terminations, were offered

      10      a funded alternative for child care in

      11      fiscal-year 2012.

      12             While many New York families were spared the

      13      loss of critical child-care services for this year,

      14      there is uncertainty about the fiscal 2013 budget.

      15             At the federal level, we are anticipating

      16      that there may be cuts in child care and Head Start,

      17      as part of the overall deficit-reduction package, if

      18      there is no agreement on appropriations.

      19             Such a cut would only exacerbate the fiscal

      20      pressures on child care and Head Start.

      21             Despite these challenges, the City

      22      continues to contribute more than its share

      23      required by the Child Care and Development Block

      24      Grant, as we provide child care to families

      25      receiving cash assistance, and are committed to





 

                                                                   11
       1      providing child care to low-income families.

       2             In order to sustain, and allow for its

       3      sustainability of the system, it is essential that

       4      there be additional State funding for child care

       5      across New York.

       6             In addition, we would like to work jointly

       7      with you to advocate for federal funds, to prevent

       8      further cuts, or maintain an increased federal

       9      funding for the Child-Care Development Block Grant.

      10             I would also like to say a few words about

      11      Early Learn NYC.

      12             While we are limited in what we can say at

      13      this time because of the ongoing procurement and the

      14      evaluations of the proposals processed, we are

      15      excited about the response to our request for our

      16      proposal, our "RFP," from providers who are

      17      interested in administering Early Learn NYC.

      18             Children Services received proposals for

      19      more sites and seats than is our current

      20      capacity.

      21             We acknowledge, and research demonstrates,

      22      that success in school, and in life, positively

      23      associated with the experience of high-quality

      24      child care.

      25             As a result, Children Services strongly





 

                                                                   12
       1      believes that Early Learn NYC will strengthen

       2      children's development and educational experiences

       3      by setting higher standards to improve the program

       4      quality, leading to positive outcomes for

       5      children.

       6             Although there are different program

       7      requirements reflecting varying standards and

       8      regulations, the primary goals of Early Learn NYC

       9      are to better support working families and

      10      parents, and to offer high-quality child care

      11      regardless of program setting or design.

      12             This means, that no matter where a child may

      13      go for early care and education services, they'll be

      14      receiving the same level of quality services.

      15             We are currently reviewing proposals, and we

      16      anticipate notifying proposers of awards in the

      17      spring of 2012, with new contracts to begin

      18      October of 2012.

      19             A new innovative program is not necessarily

      20      easy to launch, and we have heard some concerns

      21      from members of the community.

      22             While we face some challenges, we intend to

      23      move forward with our commitment to implement

      24      Early Learn NYC, and look forward to working with

      25      community and our contractors to implement the





 

                                                                   13
       1      vision of Early Learn NYC.

       2             I would now like to turn our attention to a

       3      critical policy issue concerning comprehensive

       4      background checks.

       5             As you know, State law provides for subsidy

       6      payments to providers of informal legally exempt

       7      care, which is home-based child care not offered

       8      through a program licensed by the New York City

       9      Department of Mental Health and Hygiene.

      10             While Children Services understands the

      11      need for informal care, and that many of these

      12      providers are family members, friends, and

      13      neighbors, we do have concerns about the

      14      potential health and safety risks of children in

      15      such care.

      16             State law prohibits Children Services from

      17      fingerprinting an informal provider in order to

      18      conduct a criminal-history records search, and from

      19      requesting a search of the State Central Register;

      20      or "SCR."

      21             In contrast, such searches are conducted, and

      22      required, for all licensed providers.

      23             Currently, Children Services is limited to

      24      the background checks of informal providers

      25      allowed by State regulations.





 

                                                                   14
       1             State regulations only enable a child-welfare

       2      search, which gives us information on whether a

       3      child was removed from the provider's care, or

       4      whether a provider's parental rights were terminated

       5      for any children.

       6             This search, however, does not tell us

       7      whether a provider has an indicated report of abuse

       8      or neglect against a child.

       9             In order to obtain that information, we would

      10      need to do a search of the SCR, which State law does

      11      not allow.

      12             In addition, while State regulations require

      13      a search of the State Sex Offender's Registry to

      14      identify whether a provider or anyone in the

      15      provider home is a registered sex offender in

      16      New York State, it does not include information from

      17      other states.

      18             Recently, at the request of

      19      Children Services, the New York State Office of

      20      Children and Families approved for New York City the

      21      ability to do limited criminal-background checks.

      22             These checks consist of searching the

      23      New York State Office of Court Administration

      24      database, to identify providers with a conviction

      25      or arrest, especially for a violent crime or for a





 

                                                                   15
       1      crime against children in New York State.

       2             To better ensure our children are taken care

       3      of in a safe environment, however, there are

       4      additional critical categories that we are still not

       5      able to detect:  Indicated reports of child abuse or

       6      neglect, convictions of crimes -- of crimes

       7      outside the state, and convictions by providers

       8      using a false identity.

       9             Children Services has very serious concerns

      10      about the possibility that children may be cared for

      11      in homes where the provider, and other adults in

      12      the home, may have indicated reports of child abuse

      13      and neglect, and may have been convicted of crimes

      14      out of state, including, possibly, violent crimes.

      15             Recent federal guidance from the Office of

      16      Child Care supports Children Services' position that

      17      we should be able to access this additional

      18      information.

      19             The U.S. Department of Health and Human

      20      Services' Administration for Children and Families,

      21      strongly recommends that all providers, regardless

      22      of whether they are required to be licensed, undergo

      23      comprehensive background checks.  This includes,

      24      fingerprinting, to check state and FBI

      25      criminal-history records, as well as state child





 

                                                                   16
       1      abuse and neglect registries.

       2             Moreover, fingerprinting is the only certain

       3      tool able to detect possible fraud by providers,

       4      who may be using false identities, social security

       5      numbers, and other documentation.

       6             We, therefore, appeal to the

       7      State Legislature to amend the State Social Services

       8      Law, to allow local-services districts to:

       9             One:  Conduct an SCR clearance, to determine

      10      whether individuals applying to be legally exempt

      11      child-care providers, and persons older than

      12      18 living in the provider home, have an indicated

      13      report of child abuse or neglect;

      14             And, two:  Fingerprint the same, so that a

      15      criminal-background check can be done that would

      16      include convictions outside of New York State.

      17             Children Services has also concerns about

      18      safeguarding the rights of providers.

      19      Children Services would ensure that background

      20      checks be conducted in compliance with the

      21      New York State Human Rights Law.

      22             The ability to do these checks should not

      23      be an unfunded mandate.  Just as critical to

      24      ensuring the health and safety of children, is the

      25      commitment to provide the resources to meet that





 

                                                                   17
       1      goal.

       2             We urge the Legislature to amend the State

       3      law, so that children cared for in all types of

       4      child-care settings, including care exempt from

       5      licensing, receive the same level of protection.

       6             Safe and high-quality child care is a primary

       7      concern for parents trying to maintain their

       8      jobs and support their families.

       9             As the State invests in job growth, it is

      10      equally important to invest in child care to support

      11      parents in their efforts to work.

      12             Children Services and the City of New York

      13      are committed to providing sufficient high-quality

      14      child care to meet the needs of families in the city

      15      that require child care.

      16             We are requesting funding from the State to

      17      keep pace with increasing costs we have described,

      18      so that we are able to continue to serve the

      19      children currently in care, and are not faced with

      20      another overwhelming deficit that would force us to

      21      eliminate large numbers of child-care subsidies.

      22             Furthermore, we would welcome the opportunity

      23      to work with you, to advocate in Washington for

      24      additional federal funding for child care.

      25             We know that the State Senate shares the





 

                                                                   18
       1      City's commitment to providing high-quality

       2      child care to all families that require it.

       3             We look forward to working with you, with the

       4      Legislature, to address challenges, and the issues

       5      that I have described today.

       6             Thank you for the opportunity to speak here

       7      today before you, and I am happy to answer any

       8      questions you may have.

       9             SENATOR SAVINO:  Thank you, Ms. Vechiotti.

      10             I'm glad to hear that the administration is

      11      committed to working with the Senate, and I'm

      12      assuming, the Assembly, in trying to advocate for

      13      more child-care funding.

      14             You're absolutely correct in the assertion,

      15      that, the role of government, right now, seems to be

      16      in job creation.

      17             And I said this very clearly to the

      18      Governor's Office, that, you cannot have a

      19      job-creation program that doesn't also have the

      20      supports in place that make work pay.

      21             Child-care -- accessed, affordable,

      22      subsidized day care -- is critically important to

      23      that effort.

      24             So, I'm a little concerned, though, about

      25      this movement towards informal day care.  I think





 

                                                                   19
       1      that's a count -- I think that's actually

       2      counterproductive.

       3             And while I realize it has a role to play in

       4      day care, I think we need to do more to expand

       5      access to subsidized day care, and grow it, as

       6      opposed to shrink it.

       7             But let's -- let's get to the -- before we

       8      get to the issues on Early Learn, which is what so

       9      many people here, today, really want to hear about,

      10      in an effort to maintain the subsidized day-care

      11      slots for working families, which we all agree is

      12      critically important, especially for low-wage

      13      working women, I have a piece of legislation that

      14      I've been working on for the past year, that would

      15      exempt women who are on public assistance, with

      16      children under the age of 1, from participating in

      17      work -- in the workfare, because, as you pointed

      18      out, they are the only people that are guaranteed

      19      subsidized day care.

      20             It would save the State of New York a

      21      considerable amount of money in day care, which

      22      would help plug the holes for your agency, and

      23      other county organizations around the state; and it

      24      would preserve subsidized day care for working women

      25      who so desperately depend upon it.





 

                                                                   20
       1             So, while I'm looking forward to working with

       2      you guys on trying to get more money from the

       3      federal government for day care, I hope you will

       4      work with me in convincing the Legislature and the

       5      Governor that this is the right step to take.

       6             So, we'll talk about that more in the future,

       7      but let's get to Early Learn.

       8             We submitted to the -- for those of you in

       9      the audience, we submitted to the Commissioner, a

      10      series of questions around the Early Learn program.

      11      Many of those questions came from the provider

      12      organizations that are here, with some concerns.

      13             The agency has responded to the vast majority

      14      of them, to the best of their ability.  They feel

      15      that there's some ethical issues around the fact

      16      that there is an active RFP process out there.

      17             But, I think they gave us some -- many

      18      comprehensive answers, and we're going to go through

      19      them right now.

      20             So, that being said, the first question that

      21      we did submit to you, was:  Was there a list of

      22      organizations that had submitted proposals, and

      23      would this meet this current system capacity?

      24             SARA VECHIOTTI:  So, Early Learn NYC is a

      25      competitively sealed procurement.  And, currently,





 

                                                                   21
       1      ACS is reviewing their proposals that we received

       2      for Early Learn; and, so, therefore, the list of

       3      proposals cannot be made public.

       4             But we can tell you, that the total capacity

       5      that was proposed, in terms of unique proposers,

       6      in terms of the number of sites and the number of

       7      seats, actually exceeds the current system

       8      capacity we have today.

       9             SENATOR SAVINO:  What is the system capacity

      10      today?  Do you know?

      11             SARA VECHIOTTI:  In terms of the number of

      12      center-based slots?

      13             SENATOR SAVINO:  Uh-huh.

      14             SARA VECHIOTTI:  One second.

      15             SENATOR SAVINO:  If any of them know?

      16             You have some people.

      17             UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER:  [Inaudible.]

      18             SENATOR SAVINO:  You're looking for it there,

      19      Mr. Cartieri (ph.)?

      20                  [Laughter.]

      21             UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER:  [Inaudible.]

      22             SARA VECHIOTTI:  So, when you look at our

      23      total system, which includes both child care and

      24      Head Start, and all of our settings, it's,

      25      approximately, 50,000 seats today.





 

                                                                   22
       1             SENATOR SAVINO:  50,000.

       2             SARA VECHIOTTI:  That includes family child

       3      care and center-based care.

       4             SENATOR SAVINO:  Okay, and that doesn't take

       5      into consideration the informal home-based

       6      neighbor --

       7             SARA VECHIOTTI:  No, this is --

       8             SENATOR SAVINO:  -- family --

       9             SARA VECHIOTTI:  No, this is just the

      10      contract-system capacity we have.  It does not

      11      include the voucher system.

      12             SENATOR SAVINO:  Do you have any idea how

      13      many people are receiving vouchers for informal

      14      care?

      15             SARA VECHIOTTI:  So, approximately, we have

      16      94,000 children enrolled today in subsidized child

      17      care.  And the number of vouchered children is --

      18             Just give me one second.

      19             The number of children enrolled with

      20      vouchers is approximately 17 -- 16,500, on the

      21      low-income side.  And, then, on the cash-assistance

      22      side, it's approximately 53,000.

      23             SENATOR SAVINO:  53,000 on the -- on the --

      24             SARA VECHIOTTI:  On the cash-assistance side.

      25             SENATOR SAVINO:  -- cash-assistance side.





 

                                                                   23
       1             SARA VECHIOTTI:  Yes, correct.

       2             SENATOR SAVINO:  Lights just went out on that

       3      one.

       4             So, that -- and that's not including the

       5      50,000 that are in center-based care right now.

       6             So total, then, capacity -- the way I would

       7      look at the capacity, is the number of children who

       8      need day care; subsidized day care, or

       9      Early Childhood, or Head Start -- would be, 105 --

      10      100 and --

      11             SARA VECHIOTTI:  The number I gave you --

      12             SENATOR SAVINO:  -- 160 --

      13             SARA VECHIOTTI:  The number I gave you

      14      before, of 94,000, includes, the cash-assistance,

      15      and the low-income, families.

      16             So, those 53,000 cash-assistance children are

      17      included already in the "94,000" number.

      18             SENATOR SAVINO:  But you have 50,000 that are

      19      in center-based care?

      20             SARA VECHIOTTI:  No.  We have 50,000 that are

      21      in, center-based, and family-and-child-care,

      22      networks, in Head Start, and in child care.

      23             So, the number of "94" does not include

      24      Head Start children.

      25             If you include Head Start children, then that

       1      total is closer to 112,000 today, enrolled.

       2             SENATOR SAVINO:  Okay, so I'm going to go

       3      back to the question:  What is the capacity that is
